hero.title: What is medical technology?
hero.subtitle: Medical technology encompasses all devices, instruments, software and procedures used to diagnose, monitor, treat or alleviate diseases. Here we explain the fundamentals – clearly and in a structured way.

definition.title: Definition
definition.p1: Medical technology is the application of engineering principles and technologies in medicine. It ranges from the simple clinical thermometer to ultrasound and X-ray equipment, ventilators, dialysis systems and large-scale imaging systems.
definition.p2: Legally, these products are referred to as medical devices. In the European Union, the Medical Device Regulation (MDR, Regulation (EU) 2017/745) defines the requirements a product must meet before it may bear the CE marking and be placed on the market.
definition.p3: Unlike a medicinal product, a medical device achieves its principal intended action not by pharmacological means but by physical means: for example through measurement, imaging, mechanical support or the delivery of energy.

importance.title: Why medical technology is so important
importance.intro: Modern medicine would be unthinkable without medical technology. At every stage of care, it helps to treat patients safely, quickly and precisely.

items.title: Early and accurate diagnosis
items.text: Imaging and laboratory diagnostic procedures make diseases visible, often long before symptoms appear.

items.title: Effective therapy
items.text: From infusion pumps to dialysis: therapy devices support or replace vital bodily functions.

items.title: Safety and monitoring
items.text: Monitoring systems record vital signs continuously and raise an alarm before a condition becomes critical.

items.title: Hygiene and patient protection
items.text: Sterilisation and reprocessing prevent infections and protect patients and staff.

items.title: Efficiency in everyday care
items.text: Good equipment speeds up workflows, relieves staff and lowers costs in the long run.

classification.title: Risk classes of medical devices
classification.intro: The MDR divides medical devices into four classes according to their risk potential. The higher the class, the stricter the requirements for evidence, testing and surveillance.

classes.name: Class I
classes.text: Non-invasive or simple products with low hazard potential.
classes.examples: Examples: wheelchairs, dressings, simple examination couches

classes.name: Class IIa
classes.text: Products with moderate risk, often active devices for diagnosis or short-term use.
classes.examples: Examples: ultrasound scanners, hearing aids, many dental instruments

classes.name: Class IIb
classes.text: Products with elevated risk, such as active devices that deliver energy or support vital functions.
classes.examples: Examples: X-ray equipment, ventilators, infusion pumps, defibrillators

classes.name: Class III
classes.text: Products with the highest risk, in particular implants and products in contact with the heart, the central circulatory system or the central nervous system.
classes.examples: Examples: pacemakers, heart valves, joint implants

areas.title: Sub-fields of medical technology
areas.intro: Medical technology can be divided into several sub-fields. In our Device Knowledge portal we present typical devices from each category.

items.title: Medical imaging
items.text: Procedures that make the inside of the body visible: ultrasound, X-ray, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging.

items.title: Laboratory diagnostics
items.text: Analysers that examine blood, urine and other samples – from the centrifuge to the fully automated analyser.

items.title: Patient monitoring
items.text: Systems that continuously record vital signs such as heart rhythm, oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

items.title: Surgical technology
items.text: Operating theatre equipment: anaesthesia machines, electrosurgery, endoscopy, surgical lights and tables.

items.title: Therapy
items.text: Devices that support bodily functions or deliver treatments: ventilation, infusion, dialysis, defibrillation.

items.title: Dental technology
items.text: Technology for the dental practice: treatment units, dental X-ray and digital impressions.

items.title: Sterilization & hygiene
items.text: Reprocessing of instruments and devices: cleaning, disinfection, packaging and sterilisation.

items.text: Medical Device Regulation – EU Regulation 2017/745 on medical devices. It defines the requirements products must meet before being placed on the market.
Confirms that a medical device meets the applicable EU requirements. For higher risk classes, a Notified Body is involved.

The German Medical Devices Law Implementation Act (MPDG) and the German Medical Devices Operator Ordinance (MPBetreibV) regulate, among other things, the obligations when operating and using medical devices.
Safety-related and metrological inspections (German: sicherheitstechnische bzw. messtechnische Kontrollen) – regular checks that are mandatory for certain devices.
Documentation for certain active medical devices: training, functional tests, maintenance and malfunctions.
Unique Device Identification – a unique product identifier for the traceability of medical devices.
